Lily and Sam want to start a book club at school.
Lily thinks everyone should read the same book so they can discuss it together.
Sam wants each person to choose a different book and recommend it to the group.
They ask their classmates what they think. Some children prefer stories, while others like books about animals or space.
The friends decide to try both ideas. In the first week, everyone brings a favorite book. In the second week, they choose one short story to read together.
After a month, they will ask the group which activities helped them discover something new.
Lily realizes that listening to different ideas can make a plan better.
A class notices that the path beside their local river is covered with litter.
At first, the students want to organize one big cleanup. Their teacher asks what might happen the following week.
They realize that removing rubbish once will not stop people from leaving more.
The class makes a plan with two parts: a supervised cleanup and a set of clear signs near the path.
They also ask the local council whether more bins could be provided.
A month later, they compare photos of the same places. Some areas look much cleaner, but rubbish still collects near the bridge.
The students decide to change the position of one sign and keep checking. They have learned to use evidence to improve a plan rather than assume the first idea will solve everything.
